papers.title: Heat and Emergency Department Operations: A Two-Decade Observational Study
papers.abstract: Emergency department (ED) crowding remains one of the most pressing challenges facing the US healthcare system; environmental factors have received little attention as determinants of ED operational performance, patient behavior, or emergency service utilization. We examined the association between maximum daily heat index and ED throughput metrics, patient behavioral outcomes, and likelihood of EMS arrival. We retrospectively analyzed 485,403 warm-season ED visits from a 22-year period at a large urban academic medical center in New England. The exposure was daily maximum heat index (ERA5-Land) for Suffolk County, Massachusetts. Primary outcomes included four ED throughput time metrics: door-to-doctor time, doctor-to-decision time, boarding time, and total ED length of stay; secondary outcomes included the left without being seen rate, leaving against medical advice rate, and likelihood of EMS arrival. Each 1{ring}F increase in heat index was associated with a 0.41% increase in door-to-doctor time (95% CI: 0.38% - 0.44%). Heat index was not significantly associated with the other three throughput metrics. At the 95{degrees}F heat index threshold, patients were 27% more likely to leave against medical advice than on days below the threshold (OR 1.27; 95% CI: 1.02 - 1.58), and had higher odds of arriving by EMS (OR 1.10; 95% CI: 1.06 - 1.15). Higher heat index was associated with longer door-to-doctor time, increased EMS arrival proportion, and higher odds of leaving against medical advice. Health systems and municipalities should characterize how hot weather affects operational performance and integrate this evidence into heat-readiness planning.

papers.title: Development and Psychometric Evaluation of the AASPIRE Social Support Scale for Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Background: Social support is associated with health, well-being, and quality of life among autistic adults, yet existing social support measures have important limitations. Many were not developed with autistic people, may be difficult for autistic adults to use, and have limited psychometric evidence in autistic populations. We evaluated the psychometric properties of the AASPIRE Social Support Scale, an autism-informed measure adapted from Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) social support scales through a community-based participatory research process. Methods: The AASPIRE Social Support Scale assesses five domains: Companionship, Emotional Support, Informational Support, Practical Support, and Social Isolation. Baseline data were analyzed from 859 autistic adults recruited through healthcare systems, disability service systems, and the broader U.S. autism community. Participants completed the measure independently (n=600), with support (n=189), or through caregiver report (n=70). We evaluated content validity, structural validity using confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency, and measurement invariance across reporting approaches. We also explored differences in social support scores by reporting approach and participant characteristics. Results: The hypothesized five-factor structure demonstrated good fit, with strong item loadings supporting the five distinct but related social support domains. Internal consistency was high for the total scale and all subscales (=0.87 to 0.95). Measurement invariance was supported across independent direct-report, supported direct-report, and caregiver report, indicating that the scale measured the underlying social support domains similarly across reporting approaches. Social support scores differed across reporting groups: participants reporting independently generally reported less support and greater isolation than participants completing the measure with support or through caregiver report. Exploratory analyses also identified differences by age and gender, but not race. Conclusions: The AASPIRE Social Support Scale is an accessible, reliable, and valid multidimensional measure of social support for autistic adults. Its comparable measurement properties across independent direct-report, supported direct-report, and caregiver report support its use in studies seeking to include autistic adults with diverse communication and support needs. The scale may be useful for evaluating social support and the effectiveness of services and interventions across heterogeneous autistic adult populations.

papers.title: Where did it go? How Information Management Practices Impact Rigor and Reproducibility in Collaborative Clinical and Translational Research
papers.abstract: Introduction: Clinical and translational research teams (CTRTs) use a vast array of information (digital artifacts used to generate, share, and retrieve data) in their collaborative work, yet information management is often devalued compared to more visible aspects of data-related work. In this second paper from the Information Management Prototype for Clinical and Translational Research (IMPACT-CTR) study, we present (1) the shared practices CTRT members implemented to manage, store, retrieve and share their information, and (2) the impact of these practices on the teams and their work. Methods: We conducted individual semi-structured interviews with 52 team members across 11 CTRTs. Results: We identified information practices that spanned research activities such as team meetings, data collection, dissemination, and overall project management. Effective management of information fostered workflow efficiency, increased shared awareness, and built confidence in the research CTRTs produced. However, inconsistent management of information slowed the workflow, created frustration, and reduced trust in the completeness of research outputs. Discussion: These results demonstrate that information practices are deeply interdependent, preserve institutional knowledge, and ultimately bolster the efficient and effective progression of scientific work. CTRTs who took time to reflect on, implement, and evaluate several lightweight practices through the research lifecycle enhanced the rigor and reproducibility of their science.

papers.title: Implementing an EHR-Integrated Quality and Safety Dashboard to Improve Inpatient Safety: Clinical Usage and Preliminary Outcomes
papers.abstract: Background: Data driven tools are increasingly used to support patient safety and quality improvement, yet evidence on the impact of integrated quality and safety dashboards remains limited. Methods: We conducted a pre to post implementation study using interrupted time series analysis to evaluate the impact of an EHR-integrated quality and safety dashboard on clinical processes and patient outcomes, among three general medicine units at a 171-bed community teaching hospital. All adult patients admitted during seven-month pre- and post-implementation periods were included. The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitalizations with at least one adverse event. Secondary and exploratory outcomes included hospital-acquired conditions, adherence to safety-related process measures, and dashboard utilization. Results: A total of 9,023 hospitalizations were included (4,640 pre-implementation; 4,383 post-implementation). The proportion of hospitalizations with at least one adverse event was similar pre-implementation (23.15%; 95% CI, 20.96 to 25.29) and post-implementation (22.97%; 95% CI, 20.86 to 25.23). CLABSI per 100 patient-days was reduced (aOR 0.47, 95% CI [0.37 to 0.60]); and exploratory analyses demonstrated decreases in slope for post-discharge venous thromboembolism (aOR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.48 to 0.91; p=0.01) and hospital-acquired pressure injury (aOR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.48 to 1.00; p=0.05). Several process measures improved, including code status confirmation, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, delirium screening, chlorhexidine bathing, and fall precautions. Conclusions: Implementation of an EHR-integrated quality and safety dashboard was associated with meaningful improvements in multiple care processes and CLABSI but not overall adverse events. These findings highlight the potential of workflow-integrated dashboards to support frontline quality improvement, while underscoring the need for additional measures to improve clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Fragmented and Underutilized: Exploring Role Variation and Ambiguity for Research Project Managers in Collaborative Team Science
papers.abstract: Introduction: Clinical and translational research (CTR) increasingly relies on collaborative and interdisciplinary research teams to translate discoveries into practical solutions. Research project managers (RPMs) often support CTR projects to ensure continual progress toward research goals, yet there is still ambiguity around what research project management is and the role RPMs play on research teams. Our study aimed to address this gap in knowledge by understanding how RPMs (1) define project management in an academic research context and (2) align on the key job responsibilities of RPMs. Methods: Survey responses from 85 academic RPMs and 14 semi-structured follow-up interviews were analyzed to characterize their perspectives and experiences. Results: Findings revealed four themes: (1) RPMs were in alignment with each other and the Project Management Institute on the definition of project management while noting distinctions between academic and industry contexts, (2) RPMs reported diverse job responsibilities despite having similar job titles, (3) RPMs struggled with role ambiguity stemming from variability in key job responsibilities, and (4) RPMs identified areas of support to improve research project management. Discussion: These findings contribute to a greater understanding of project management in academic research contexts and highlight the variable utilization of RPMs on collaborative teams. Well managed projects rarely happen naturally, but can have a large impact on research environments, team member wellbeing, and overall research productivity. By characterizing how RPMs define and enact their role, this study provides a foundation for developing resources and avenues of support that can ultimately increase the efficiency of translating research discoveries from bench to bedside.

papers.title: Strengthening Childhood Cancer Care in Nepal (DECAN-CHILD): Protocol for Evaluating Quality, Financial Burden and Health System Readiness Through a Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundStrengthening health systems in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) like Nepal is essential for equitable, high-quality diagnosis and treatment and improved survival from childhood cancer. This study aims to quantify care intervals and their determinants; assess the quality of care and 1-, 2-, and 3-year survival; quantify the costs and cost burden of childhood cancer treatment from family and health system perspectives; and to assess the capacity of health systems in Nepal to diagnose and treat children with cancer. MethodsThis three-year prospective cohort study will enrol and follow consecutive childhood cancer patients aged 0-19 years registered at six tertiary hospitals in Nepal, accounting for approximately 90% of childhood cancer cases diagnosed nationally. After obtaining informed consent and assent, a semi structured questionnaire will be administered to patient/caregiver at baseline and every three months during the first year and every six months in the second and third years. Patient/caregiver data will be supplemented with patients medical records kept in the hospital. A national capacity assessment will assess readiness for childhood cancer care in tertiary-level and secondary-level healthcare facilities involved in referral, diagnosis, treatment or shared care. Survival outcomes will be examined using Cox proportional hazards models and random effects models to account for hospital clustering. Out-of-pocket costs will be analysed using descriptive statistics and a two-part regression model to account for zero-inflated cost distributions, with five-year health system cost projections modelled to estimate corresponding rates of catastrophic health expenditure and medical impoverishment. DiscussionThis study will generate comprehensive evidence on childhood cancer care, costs, and health system capacity for care in Nepal. Findings will directly inform policy guidance, resource allocation and benefit package design for childhood cancer care in Nepal, inform comparable efforts in other low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and will contribute to Nepals efforts in the WHO Global Initiative for Childhood Cancer towards improved cancer outcomes.

papers.title: From Evidence to Intervention: A Systematic, Multi-Stakeholder Approach to Developing and Prioritizing Diagnostic Excellence Interventions Across a 14-Site Hospital Medicine Collaborative
papers.abstract: BackgroundDiagnostic errors are common and represent a leading cause of preventable harm in hospitalized medical patients. Despite growing recognition of this problem, the field lacks a systematic, evidence-based approach for developing, adapting, and selecting diagnostic excellence interventions at scale across multiple institutions. MethodsUsing a structured, multi-phase process, the Achieving Diagnostic Excellence through Prevention and Teamwork (ADEPT) collaborative, a 14-site AHRQ-funded hospital medicine network: (1) conducted an environmental scan of existing diagnostic safety practices across sites; (2) constructed a conceptual framework organizing potential interventions by target (patient, provider/team, health system) and safety paradigm (Safety I and Safety II); (3) convened multidisciplinary working groups to develop detailed proposals for six intervention programs; (4) applied a pre-specified multi-criteria rubric to facilitate group deliberation, and (5) voted to select a single high-priority intervention for collaborative launch. ResultsSix interventions were developed, selected, or adapted from prior work, spanning all cells of the target and safety paradigm framework. Finalized proposals were then shared at two separate ADEPT meetings - the first to solicit feedback on interventions and to coordinate activities across groups, and the second where a formal ranked-choice vote was held. This process resulted in selection of the Diagnostic Cross-Check (DXC) -- a structured, peer second-opinion program triggered by rapid response team (RRT) events -- as the highest priority intervention for collaborative-wide launch. The remaining interventions were designated as components of an ADEPT toolbox for future adaptation, adoption, and evaluation. DiscussionThe ADEPT collaboratives systematic, evidence-informed approach to diagnostic intervention development offers a replicable model for other multi-site quality improvement networks. The resulting portfolio of interventions provides a roadmap for the field of inpatient diagnostic excellence.

papers.title: Pharmacist-Led Comprehensive Medication Management and Patient Outcomes in Pediatric Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Multicenter Cohort Study
papers.abstract: ObjectiveClinical pharmacists improve medication management and safety in intensive care units, yet their role in neonatal and pediatric intensive care remains highly variable across institutions. Evidence supporting standardized clinical pharmacy practice models in these settings is limited. This study evaluated the association between pharmacist service coverage and clinical outcomes in critically ill pediatric patients. DesignMulticenter, observational study with prospective and retrospective data collection. SettingICUs at participating institutions in the United States and internationally. PatientsPatients <18 years of age InterventionNone MeasurementsThe primary exposure was pharmacist-led comprehensive medication management (CMM) with daily participation in multidisciplinary rounds. The secondary exposure was the pharmacist-to-ICU-patient ratio. The primary outcome was hazard of discharge alive (HDA) from the ICU. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, hospital HDA, and hazard of extubation alive (HEA). Fine-Gray competing risks models and multivariable Firth logistic regression were used for adjusted analyses. Main resultsA total of 1,459 patients cared for by 69 clinical pharmacists across 31 institutions were included. Daily CMM with rounding was associated with a higher HDA from the ICU (HR 2.60, 95% CI 2.17-3.10; p<0.001), higher HDA from the hospital (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.83-2.75; p<0.001), and a higher HEA (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.10-1.33; p<0.001), but not with in-hospital mortality (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.14-1.36; p=0.154). The pharmacist-to-ICU-patient ratio was not significantly associated with ICU HDA (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.01; p=0.88) or any secondary outcome. ConclusionsDaily pharmacist-provided CMM with multidisciplinary ICU rounding was associated with improved discharge outcomes among critically ill pediatric and neonatal patients, whereas pharmacist-to-ICU-patient ratio alone was not. These findings support standardized integration of clinical pharmacists into daily multidisciplinary rounds in this setting.

papers.title: Emergency Department Utilization Following a Community Hospital Closure: A Population-Based Comparative Study
papers.abstract: ImportanceHospital closures may alter access to emergency care. However, changes in utilization among residents of affected communities are less well characterized than changes in volume at surrounding hospitals. ObjectiveTo compare changes in emergency department (ED) utilization among Madera County residents following the closure of Madera Community Hospital (MCH) with changes among Fresno County residents, and to examine geographic differences by pre-closure reliance on MCH. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsRetrospective population-based comparative study of annual California hospital Patient Origin/Market Share data, 2015-2024, with an exploratory comparative interrupted time-series analysis. Pre-pandemic years were 2015-2019, pandemic-affected pre-closure years were 2020-2022, and the two complete closure years were 2023-2024. Encounters were classified by county of patient residence, regardless of treating hospital location. Main Outcomes and MeasuresCombined ED encounters (ED-only plus inpatient-from-ED) and each component separately. County-level utilization was expressed as encounters per 1,000 residents using annual population estimates. Geographic comparisons by pre-closure MCH dependence used ZIP-code encounter counts. ResultsFrom 2022 to 2023, the first complete year following closure, combined ED utilization declined from 398.47 to 333.61 encounters per 1,000 Madera County residents (-16.3%), compared with 399.61 to 398.49 (-0.3%) among Fresno County residents. Madera ED-only rates declined 20.4%, while inpatient-from-ED rates increased 13.4%; however, the adjusted comparative analysis did not identify a consistent additional Madera-specific increase in inpatient-from-ED utilization. Exploratory regression estimated Madera-specific closure-period rate ratios of 0.871 for combined ED utilization and 0.848 for ED-only utilization. Combined ED encounter counts declined 18.4% in high-MCH-dependence ZIP codes versus 5.8% in low-dependence ZIP codes. Statistical inference was limited by the inclusion of only two counties, two complete closure years, and substantial overdispersion. Conclusions and RelevanceThe period following MCH closure was associated with a substantial reduction in ED utilization among Madera County residents relative to Fresno County residents, concentrated in ED-only encounters and communities previously most dependent on MCH. The observational design does not establish causation or determine whether reduced utilization reflected substitution to other care settings, decreased demand, or unmet medical need.

papers.title: Why Have Drug Names Become So Weird? A Retrospective Analysis of the Orthographic Distinctiveness of Proprietary and Generic Names Across Four Decades of FDA Approvals
papers.abstract: BackgroundRegulatory pressure to avoid confusingly similar drug names appears to have pushed manufacturers to coin more distinctive proprietary names, but no one has quantitatively analyzed this trend. ObjectiveTo determine whether proprietary drug names became more orthographically distinctive (unusual in spelling) over time. MethodsWe examined 1,321 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) new molecular entity (NME) names (1985-2024), 2,769 FDA Orange Book trade names (1982-2026), 177,337 US pharmaceutical trademarks (1980-2026), and 1,273 generic names (1982-2025). Compared to prior names (including those already marketed) and ordinary English, we scored each names character trigram (three-letter sequence) surprisal (statistical unexpectedness) and its edit-distance similarity to the closest existing names. Linear regression tested time trends, controlling for name length. ResultsMean NME trigram surprisal rose in every decade between the 1980s and 2020s, from 7.21 to 8.50 nats (natural-logarithm units, higher meaning less predictable), an 18% increase (b = 0.038, p < .001, R{superscript 2} = 0.34). Half of 2020s names (7% in the 1980s) contained a letter sequence found in no common English word (e.g., Jesduvroq, Omvoh). Nearest-neighbor similarity fell after the early 1990s. Trademark data showed the same trend (b = 0.016, p < .001). Generic names showed a weaker trend (b = 0.011, R{superscript 2} = 0.063). ConclusionsOver four decades, drug names became more orthographically distinctive, consistent with namespace crowding, deliberate efforts to avoid confusing names, and branding strategy. Because unfamiliar letter sequences can introduce other error pathways, increased distinctiveness does not necessarily imply improved safety.

papers.title: Patient Perceptions of Student Involvement and Satisfaction in a Student-Run Free Clinic Serving People Experiencing Homelessness
papers.abstract: BackgroundPatient satisfaction is a key measure of healthcare quality among people experiencing homelessness. Student-run free clinics (SRFCs) provide care to underserved populations, but the role of student involvement in patient satisfaction remains unclear. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study of patients receiving care at an SRFC. From February 2024 to February 2025, patients completed post-visit surveys assessing satisfaction that were evaluated using regression analyses. ResultsEighty-eight patients completed surveys, reporting high overall satisfaction (mean 9.26/10). In separate linear regression models adjusted for age, gender, and race, greater perceived benefit of student involvement was associated with higher satisfaction ({beta} = .298, p =.037), whereas perceiving the visit as too long was associated with lower satisfaction ({beta} = -.285, p = .019). ConclusionGreater perceived benefit of student involvement was associated with higher patient satisfaction, whereas longer perceived visit duration was associated with lower satisfaction. These findings highlight the importance of balancing educational opportunities with efficient workflows in SRFCs.

papers.title: Effect of a culturally adapted birth preparedness and complication readiness training intervention on knowledge among Hehe pregnant women in rural Iringa Tanzania: A controlled pretest-posttest quasi-experimental study
papers.abstract: BackgroundBirth preparedness and complication readiness (BPCR) knowledge is important for recognizing maternal and newborn danger signs and preparing for timely care. However, conventional translation of BPCR educational materials may not adequately address local linguistic and cultural contexts. This study evaluated whether a culturally adapted Swahili BPCR training manual improved knowledge more than a standard translated Swahili BPCR training manual among Hehe pregnant women in rural Iringa, Tanzania. MethodsA controlled pretest-posttest quasi-experimental study was conducted among 176 pregnant women attending antenatal care in Mufindi and Kilolo districts. Eighty-eight women received the Culturally Adapted Swahili BPCR Training Manual and 88 received the Standard Translated Swahili BPCR Training Manual. Both groups received comparable BPCR education with standardized session duration, delivery format, language, and follow-up procedures. BPCR knowledge was assessed using a 64-item questionnaire at baseline and four weeks after the intervention. The primary analysis used Difference-in-Differences regression to compare changes in knowledge between groups. Multiple linear regression was used to assess the association between intervention-group assignment and post-intervention knowledge after adjustment for baseline knowledge and participant characteristics. ResultsAll 176 participants completed both assessments. Mean knowledge scores increased from 21.01 (SD 7.42) to 38.49 (SD 7.54) in the culturally adapted group and from 22.51 (SD 5.80) to 32.81 (SD 5.55) in the standard translated group. The culturally adapted group demonstrated a 7.18-point greater increase in knowledge than the standard translated group ({beta} = 7.18, 95% CI: 4.40-9.97; p < 0.001). After adjustment for baseline knowledge, age, education, gravidity, marital status, living arrangement, reading ability, and occupation, intervention-group assignment remained significantly associated with higher post-intervention knowledge ({beta} = 5.88, 95% CI: 3.84-7.92; p < 0.001). ConclusionCulturally adapted BPCR education was associated with greater short-term improvement in knowledge than standard translated education among Hehe pregnant women. Integrating culturally and linguistically appropriate terminology, contextual explanations, and locally meaningful communication into BPCR education may strengthen knowledge outcomes. Multisite studies with stronger allocation procedures and longer follow-up are needed to confirm these findings. Trial RegistrationPan African Clinical Trials Registry: PACTR202607626025411. Registered retrospectively on 09 July 2026.

papers.title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
papers.abstract: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical gold standard in Germany. In a first step developing the method and demonstrating its potential we developed a representative set of patient vignettes and compared two regulated medical-device triage systems, SmED and Infermedica, with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories-emergency, acute, and not urgent-and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.5-66.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment. Broader expert consensus and evaluation, as well as further steps to reduce dependence on SmED-derived source data, are needed and planned before drawing conclusions about clinical safety.

papers.title: Innovations, recipients, and contexts in the implementation of pediatric neurocritical care programs: a multisite qualitative study refining i-PARIHS
papers.abstract: BackgroundPediatric neurocritical care (PNCC) has emerged as a distinct field, and many hospitals have moved to establishing dedicated PNCC programs. How practice change is implemented within these programs is not well understood. This study had two objectives. First, we sought to understand the barriers and facilitators of practice change in PNCC from the perspectives of the multiprofessional clinicians who deliver it. Second, we sought to characterize how well the integrated Promoting Action on Research Implementation in Health Services (i-PARIHS) implementation determinant framework captures them. MethodsWe conducted semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample of clinicians involved in PNCC at three U.S. academic medical centers. The interview guide was developed using i-PARIHS to organize barriers and facilitators of practice change across the innovation, recipients, context, and facilitation constructs. We applied framework analysis, combining deductive i-PARIHS, study-specific, and inductively derived categories. Two coders independently indexed the transcripts and reconciled them to consensus, with first-author adjudication. Preliminary site-level findings were validated with participants. ResultsWe interviewed 33 clinicians: 24 physicians, 7 nurses, and 2 advanced practice providers. Most determinants of practice change mapped to existing i-PARIHS constructs, but three were not adequately captured by the framework as currently specified. The most consequential was an interprofessional authority gradient that determined whose preferences prevailed when intensive care, neurology, and neurosurgery disagreed. The other two were clinician autonomy, which served as the lens through which the acceptability of a change was judged, and the affective state clinicians bring to practice change. Receptivity depended more on recipients values, prior experience, and capacity to absorb change into a demanding workflow. Facilitation was variable, frequently under-resourced, and dependent on credibility across professional groups. We translated these findings into three propositions linked to implementation strategies and outcomes. ConclusionsParticipants attributed practice change in PNCC more to the recipients of change, the multiprofessional context, and the availability of facilitation than to the strength of evidence for a given practice. i-PARIHS captured most barriers and facilitators well but may be adapted in this setting. Credible, resourced, authority-sensitive facilitation may improve the prospects for sustained practice change as institutions develop PNCC programs. Contributions to the literatureO_LIDeterminant frameworks are widely used but rarely revised once published; this study supports three i-PARIHS framework modifications potentially applicable to the general pediatric ICU and PNCC programs regarding clinician autonomy, the affective state clinicians bring to change, and the interprofessional authority gradient. C_LIO_LIWe identify authority-sensitive facilitation as an important driver of sustained practice change amongst multispecialty teams. C_LIO_LIWe offer three i-PARIHS elaborations with linked implementation outcomes and implications for selecting implementation strategies for teams with shared authority across professions. C_LI

papers.title: Researchers Behavioral Intentions to Engage in Knowledge Translation Activities and Their Association with Bibliometric Indicators: A Theory of Planned Behavior-Informed Questionnaire Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundKnowledge translation (KT) is essential for ensuring that research evidence informs policy and practice. However, little is known about researchers intentions to engage in KT activities or their relationship with conventional bibliometric indicators. This study aimed to (1) assess researchers intentions to engage in KT activities using a questionnaire informed by the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), and (2) examine the association between these intentions and individual bibliometric indicators. MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted among faculty members at Tehran University of Medical Sciences. A questionnaire informed by selected constructs of the TPB was developed to assess researchers intentions to engage in activities across the seven components the action cycle of Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework. The instrument was validated through several rounds of expert review and then with a sample of potential participants. Bibliometric indicators (H-index, Number of Publications, Number of Citations, First-Author Publications, Corresponding Authorship, International Publications and Self-Citations) were extracted from the national academic registry. To assess representativeness, bibliometric characteristics of respondents were compared with those of a random sample of non-respondents drawn from the same registry. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) validated the intention construct, and Structural Equation Modeling examined associations with demographic and bibliometric variables. ResultsA total of 143 researchers participated. Intention scores were highest for adapting knowledge to local contexts and identifying barriers and facilitators, and lowest for monitoring and sustaining knowledge use. CFA supported a unidimensional intention construct with favorable model-fit indicators. No bibliometric indicator was significantly associated with KT intention. Age was the only significant predictor. Respondents had stronger bibliometric profiles than non-respondents, indicating potential non-response bias. ConclusionsResearchers reported relatively strong intentions to engage in KT, but these intentions were not associated with conventional bibliometric indicators. Age was the only significant predictor. Overall, findings suggest that traditional academic metrics may not reflect KT intentions and highlight the need to strengthen institutional incentives for KT.

papers.title: Characterization of Medication-Related Errors and Prioritization of Patient-Safety Interventions in Hospital Care: A Retrospective Observational Study
papers.abstract: A. RationaleMedication-related incidents are an important patient-safety concern, particularly in critical-care and inpatient settings where polypharmacy, clinical complexity, frequent therapeutic modifications, and transitions of care increase the risk of medication errors. Systematic analysis of reported incidents can help identify predominant error patterns, potential contributing factors, and priority areas for quality improvement. The present study was undertaken to characterize medication-related incidents and identify areas requiring targeted patient-safety interventions. B. Research QuestionWhat are the predominant patterns and distribution of medication-related incidents across critical-care and inpatient units, what patient-care, process, communication, documentation, and system-level factors potentially contribute to their occurrence, and how can these findings be systematically translated into prioritized, evidence-based quality-improvement interventions to strengthen medication safety and reduce preventable medication-related harm? C. Study Design and MethodsA retrospective descriptive observational study was conducted to assess the pattern of medication-related errors identified through medication audits conducted in inpatient and critical-care settings. A total of 74 medication audit records were retrospectively reviewed. Each record was evaluated for the presence and type of medication-related error, including transcription, administration, documentation, and dispensing errors. The identified medication errors were categorized based on the nature of the error documented in the audit records. As individual records could contain more than one type of medication-related error, the error categories were considered non-mutually exclusive. Consequently, the total number of error occurrences could exceed the number of records reviewed. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed using frequency distributions and percentages to determine the relative occurrence of each medication-error category. Pareto analysis was subsequently performed to identify the predominant error categories and establish priorities for quality-improvement interventions. The Pareto analysis demonstrated that transcription and administration errors constituted the major contributors to the observed medication-related errors. The identified error patterns were further evaluated using a process-based patient-safety approach to determine potential failure points within the medication-use process. Poka-Yoke (error-proofing) principles were applied to identify opportunities for preventing or detecting errors at the point of occurrence. Based on the findings, potential interventions included standardization of medication-ordering and transcription processes, mandatory verification of medication details, strengthening of independent verification for high-alert medications, and incorporation of technology-enabled safeguards such as electronic medication administration records and barcode-based medication administration. The findings were used to identify priority areas for targeted quality-improvement interventions aimed at reducing medication-related errors and strengthening the safety and reliability of the medication-use process. D. ResultsA total of 91 medication-related error occurrences were identified across the 74 audit records reviewed. Transcription errors constituted the predominant error category (46; 50.5%), followed by administration-related errors (41; 45.1%). Documentation-related and dispensing-related errors accounted for 3 (3.3%) and 1 (1.1%) occurrences, respectively. Pareto analysis demonstrated that transcription and administration-related errors collectively accounted for 87 of the 91 identified occurrences (95.6%), indicating a substantial concentration of medication-related errors within these two categories. The cumulative frequency increased from 50.5% for transcription errors to 95.6% following inclusion of administration-related errors, while the remaining categories contributed only 4.4% of the total error occurrences. Accordingly, transcription and administration-related errors were identified as the principal priority areas for subsequent root cause analysis and quality-improvement interventions. InterpretationThe findings demonstrate that transcription errors (50.5%) and administration-related errors (45.1%) were the predominant medication-related errors, collectively accounting for 87 of the 91 identified error occurrences (95.6%). Documentation-related errors constituted 3.3%, while dispensing-related errors accounted for 1.1% of the observed occurrences. Pareto analysis revealed a marked concentration of medication-related errors within the transcription and administration domains, indicating that these two categories represented the principal areas requiring focused quality-improvement interventions. Subsequent Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and Poka-Yoke-based error-proofing approaches were therefore directed toward identifying and mitigating process vulnerabilities within these high-frequency error domains.

papers.title: Medicine carbon footprinting across National Health Service trusts in England, 2021-2024: a longitudinal study using Freedom of Information requests
papers.abstract: IntroductionMedicines account for 20% of the National Health Service (NHS) carbon footprint, but it is unclear how consistently they are measured by individual NHS trusts. This study assessed medicine carbon footprint (MCF) practices across NHS trusts in England and whether these changed between 2021 and 2024. MethodsFreedom of Information requests were sent to NHS trusts about MCF practices in 2021 and 2024. Responses were analysed to determine the proportion of trusts calculating MCFs, the medicines included and the emission factors used for spend-based calculations. Reported spend-based factors were compared with the median factor for each year to assess the effect of factor choice on MCFs. ResultsOf 196 trusts included in analysis, 178 (91%) responded for 2021 and 182 (93%) for 2024. Among responding trusts, 30 of 178 calculated MCFs in 2021 compared with 46 of 182 in 2024. Spend-based medicine footprinting increased from 19 trusts in 2021 to 31 in 2024. Ten different factors were used by 15 trusts in 2021 and 13 by 21 trusts in 2024. Reported factors ranged from 31% below to 258% above the median in 2024. ConclusionsMedicine carbon footprinting remained uncommon, with only one-quarter of responding NHS trusts calculating a footprint in 2024. Among trusts using spend-based methods, wide variation in emission factors produced substantially different estimated MCFs. Clear national guidance on spend-based methodology could improve consistency in the short term, while greater use of standardised product-level approaches may better support medicine decarbonisation over time.

papers.title: Effectiveness of a mHealth nutrition and lifestyle intervention (mHENAL) in reducing Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Sri Lankan adults: A Randomized Control Trial
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are the leading cause of global mortality, responsible for 17.8 million deaths and 423 million prevalent cases annually. While the etiology of CVD is multifactorial, evidence confirms that multicomponent behavioral interventions regarding diet and lifestyle can substantially reduce risk. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a 12-month mHealth intervention, i.e., public health practice supported by mobile devices in reducing the 10-year CVD risk among overweight and obese adults aged 35 to 64 in an urban Sri Lankan population. A two-group parallel-arm randomized control trial (RCT) was conducted with 1,200 participants from the Colombo district, assigned either to an intervention arm (n=600) or a usual care control arm (n=600). The intervention group received automated text and voice messages in their native language at a frequency of two of each per week over 12 months. The primary outcome, 10-year CVD risk, was assessed using the WHO CVD risk prediction score. The intervention significantly reduced the proportion of participants with a 10-year CVD risk from 10.0% to 6.2% (p=0.003), whereas no significant change was observed in the control group (11.0% to 9.7%). Participants in the mHealth arm demonstrated substantial behavioral improvements, including increasing daily fruit and vegetable servings from 3.6 to 5.5 and reducing daily salt intake from 7.64g to 5.62g. Physical activity levels also improved, with 89.6% meeting minimum daily requirements compared to 77.4% at baseline. These findings suggest a potentially beneficial effect on predicted cardiovascular risk. The study concludes that an automated mHealth intervention is an effective, feasible, and acceptable approach to reducing cardiovascular risk in an urban South Asian setting. The findings provide a robust evidence base for integrating digital health strategies into national non-communicable disease (NCD) prevention policies. While the 12-month results are promising, further longitudinal research is required to evaluate the long-term sustainability of these behavioral changes and their ultimate impact on mortality rates. Competing interestsThere are no competing interests Author ApprovalAll authors have seen and approved the manuscript.

papers.title: A Methodology to Evaluate the Efficacy and Patient-Centeredness of a Patient-Facing AI Chatbot: Development and Validation of a Standardized-Patient Method
papers.abstract: BackgroundPatient-facing AI intake chatbots can enter clinical use without regulatory review, so their errors may first surface with actual patients. ObjectiveTo develop and pilot a remote, voice-based standardized patient (SP) method for evaluating an intake chatbots history-taking, documentation, and patient-centeredness. MethodsFour primary care cases had Easy and Difficult variants. In Phase 1, five SPs completed 40 encounters with internal medicine residents rating portrayal fidelity. In Phase 2, SPs completed 80 encounters with a ChatGPT 4o chatbot, recorded whether critical elements were asked about and addressed satisfactorily, and rated summaries; four debriefing interviews were analyzed. In Phase 3, two blinded clinicians rated transcripts and summaries from 101 encounters (32 resident-led, 69 chatbot-led). ResultsPortrayal fidelity averaged 4.52 of 5. The chatbot asked about 59.3% of critical elements in Easy versus 50.2% in Difficult variants (adjusted OR 1.49; 95% CI, 1.15 to 1.93) and addressed 73.3% versus 64.6% (OR 1.47; 1.12 to 1.93); near-ceiling summary quality did not differ. SPs reported missed information and rushed pacing. Reviewer agreement was moderate to substantial for element judgments (AC1 0.49 to 0.70) but poor for totals (ICC 0.10 and 0.21). In exploratory comparisons, residents asked about more elements (adjusted difference 12.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 7.0 to 18.1) and satisfactorily addressed more (9.2 points; 3.8 to 14.6); totals did not differ. ConclusionsSP portrayal was consistent enough for pre-clinical chatbot evaluation, and the method detected lower coverage in harder cases. Documentation ratings alone may miss conversational gaps, which require direct measurement.

papers.title: Learning-by-Doing to Adapt a Digital Community Engagement Strategy for Identifying and Reaching Zero-Dose Children in Kano State, Nigeria: A Program Case Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundKano State has one of the highest concentrations of zero-dose (ZD) children in Nigeria, challenging equitable immunization coverage. Digital engagement tools meant to strengthen timely data to address such gaps often underperform due to limited adaptability to user needs. Learning-by-doing (LxD), which brings together human-centered design and adaptive management, offers more context-responsive solutions. Intervention and Implementation ApproachMCH-Track, a digital platform for tracking and referral for childhood vaccinations was used by 56 female community mobilizers in two local government areas (LGAs) out of the 44 LGAs in Kano State, Nigeria. We conducted a program case study from: 1) August 2024-April 2025 (initial implementation); and 2) adapted implementation (May 2025-November 2025), where LxD was incorporated to address emergent challenges. LxD included structured shadowing, monthly interviews with users, after-action reviews, and change log to track adaptations alongside routine services. Performance was monitored using four indicators: feedback actioned, response time-to-user feedback, ease-of-use score, and mobilizer performance in tracking ZD children. FindingsAfter incorporating LxD, 17 issues were identified and led to 12 prioritized adaptations. All logged issues received responses, with median response time declining to approximately two weeks, while community mobilizers reported higher usability of the digital platform (e.g., mean ease-of-use score of 4.1 out of 5). Enhanced root-cause analysis enabled trend tracking and clearer escalation pathways for systemic issues like micro-stockouts at immunization points. Empathy tool records revealed mobilizer struggles with platform. This was immediately logged, prompting user experience redesign into a seamless, single-step process from registration-to-referral. During the LxD implementation period, an average of 33 ZD children per month were identified via MCH-Track, a substantial increase from the pre-LxD period (an average of 11 ZD children identified per month). Average referral-to-access rates also improved during the LxD period, rising from 44% of identified and referred ZD children accessing immunization services pre-LxD to 70% after incorporating LxD practices. ConclusionEmbedding LxD within MCH-Track strengthened co-creation, streamlined workflows, and improved community mobilizer performance, demonstrating the value of adaptive management in reaching ZD children. Teaser MessageIntegrating learning-by-doing approaches - mixture of human-centered design and adaptive management - into a digital community-engagement platform improved understanding of previously under-recognized vaccination barriers, implementing locally tailored adaptations, and strengthening frontline responsiveness to reach zero-dose children in Kano State, Nigeria. Key MessagesO_ST_ABSKey FindingsC_ST_ABSO_LICo-creation with community mobilizers and transparent change log use translated frontline feedback into trackable system improvements, improved birth-registration-to-referral workflows, and enhanced identification and follow-up of zero-dose children. C_LIO_LIEmbedding iterative rapid cycles within the digital community-engagement platform addressed weak feedback loops and unified decisions between mobilizers and supervisors. C_LIO_LIIncorporating monthly learn-by-doing cycles into MCH-Track implementation strengthened how community mobilizers helped households overcome vaccination barriers through root-cause-analysis. For instance, insights from After-Action Reviews revealed "programmatic mistrust" was linked to "male-resistance", a key barrier to vaccination. C_LI Key ImplicationsO_LIHealth system managers and implementing partners could benefit from incorporating learn-by-doing approaches - human-centered design plus adaptive management - into existing platforms (e.g, Health Partners Forums) and prioritizing co-creation with communities who face challenges with services, gender dynamics, and trust. C_LIO_LIProgram managers can combine digital tools with structured feedback cycles to better identify and respond to healthcare worker needs, increase efficiency and quality. C_LIO_LIEmbedding adaptive learning processes within routine immunization governance and financing structures could promote more responsive and resilient programming. C_LI

papers.title: Carrying Bangladesh with Them: How Pre-Migration Healthcare Norms Shape Bangladeshi Immigrants' Health-Seeking in the United States
papers.abstract: Bangladeshi immigrants are a rapidly growing U.S. immigrant population, yet little is known about how pre-migration healthcare experiences shape healthcare use after migration. This qualitative study explored how healthcare norms from Bangladesh influence Bangladeshi immigrants health-seeking behaviors in the U.S., the barriers and facilitators they encounter, and their perceptions of care quality. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 29 Bangladeshi-born adults living in the U.S. from September 2020 to January 2021 and analyzed using the constant comparative method. Participants described healthcare expectations shaped by Bangladeshs out-of-pocket, resource-limited system, including symptom-driven rather than preventive care, self-treatment, and family-based caregiving. In the U.S., they faced barriers such as insurance confusion, long waits, difficulty establishing care, coverage disruptions, financial concerns, and language challenges. While participants valued culturally and linguistically concordant care, preferences for Bangla-speaking or co-ethnic providers varied, especially when perceived quality was low. Community networks, online information, self-education, and self-advocacy helped facilitate care. Provider communication strongly shaped perceptions of U.S. healthcare: feeling heard, respected, and well-informed promoted trust, while dismissal or delayed diagnosis led to skepticism and avoidance. These findings suggest that Bangladeshi immigrants healthcare engagement is shaped by both structural barriers and pre-migration norms. Improving access will require attention to subgroup-specific histories, insurance navigation, language access, and the relational quality of care.

papers.title: Evaluating the Synergistic Impact of Digital Logistics Systems (eLMIS) and Financial Auditing (APTS) on Essential Commodity Availability in Ethiopian Public Healthcare Facilities: A Multilevel Analysis of the 2024/2025 National Survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundChronic pharmaceutical stock outs hinder Universal Health Coverage in Ethiopia. To address this, the Ministry of Health introduced the electronic Logistics Management Information System for inventory visibility and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services for financial management. However, no national study has tested their combined impact. This study evaluated the individual and synergistic effects of electronic Logistics Management Information System and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services on essential commodity availability across Ethiopian public healthcare facilities. MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of the 2024/2025 Ethiopian Service Provision Assessment dataset utilizing 1245 public facilities nested within 125 clusters. The primary outcome was optimal essential commodity availability (zero stock outs and 100% tracer commodity presence). A two-level mixed-effects logistic regression model with an interaction term evaluated synergy, reporting Adjusted Odds Ratios with 95% Confidence Intervals. ResultsOverall optimal availability was 54.2% (95% CI; 51.4%-57.0%). Implementation rates were 41.2% for eLMIS, 38.2% for APTS and 26.5% for dual implementation. Facilities using eLMIS alone (AOR = 2.15; 95% CI: 1.52-3.04) and APTS alone (AOR = 1.82; 95% CI; 1.28-2.58) showed higher security. Dual implementation showed a profound synergistic effect (AOR = 4.32; 95% CI; 3.25-5.74, p < 0.001). Positive predictors included functional cold chains (AOR = 2.08), qualified staffing (AOR = 1.68), hub proximity (AOR = 1.58) and urban settings (AOR = 1.95). The model explained 66.2% of regional variance. ConclusionDual implementation of electronic Logistics Management Information System and Auditable Pharmaceutical Transactions and Services creates a powerful synergistic impact on pharmaceutical availability. Synchronized national scale-up and cold chain investments are urgently needed to achieve supply chain resilience and Universal Health Coverage in Ethiopia.

papers.title: Defining Manuscript Peer Review: An International Delphi Consensus Study
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo conduct a Delphi process to inform an international, consensus definition of manuscript peer review. DesignThree-round Delphi consensus study including two surveys and one virtual consensus meeting. Peer review features identified through a prior scoping review were rated on a 5-point Likert scale in Rounds 1 and 2 and voted on using include, exclude, and abstain options in Round 3. Consensus was defined as [≥]80% agreement. SettingInternational experts representing interest holders affected by manuscript peer review across the fields of biomedical, health, and social sciences, economics, and healthcare-related industries. ParticipantsRound 1 participants were purposively recruited via email from corresponding authors of articles included in the preceding scoping review. Round 2 participants were those who completed Round 1. Round 3 participants were purposely selected to address gaps in representation from earlier rounds, with attention to diversity of perspectives and equity-relevant characteristics informed by PROGRESS-Plus (e.g., geographic location, gender, race/ethnicity, occupation, and socioeconomic context). Participants were required to communicate in English. Main outcome measuresConsensus on the terminology, scope, characteristics, functions, processes, and reviewer characteristics that should inform a definition of manuscript peer review. ResultsAcross the three rounds (N=143, 109, and 16 participants, respectively), 44 peer review features across six domains (Characteristics, Function, Motivation, Assessment, Process, and Challenges) and six peer reviewer characteristics met the consensus threshold for inclusion. Consensus was also reached on terminology to describe manuscript peer review and the peer review workflow. Results were synthesized into a final conceptualization of manuscript peer review, consisting of one definition and eight pillars.The consensus definition is: "Manuscript peer review is a structured process by which human reviewers assess scholarly manuscripts, with the aim of improving the quality and trustworthiness of published research in line with norms of reciprocity to the research community." The eight pillars characterize manuscript peer review and are as follows: Principled, Constructive, Timely, Transparent, Professional, Quality, Confidential, and Pluralistic. ConclusionsThis three-round international Delphi established a consensus-based, normative conceptualization of manuscript peer review as a distinct, human-led process to improve the quality and trustworthiness of scholarly research. The resulting definition and eight pillars may provide a shared foundation for research, evaluation, education, and improvement across publishing contexts while allowing operational features to remain adaptable.

papers.title: HealthFound: a health world model for quantitative reasoning on longitudinal health profiles
papers.abstract: Medical large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in medical knowledge retrieval and clinical reasoning. However, their capacity for quantitative reasoning over dense, longitudinal health data remains limited, largely due to the lack of effective training strategies that leverage large-scale, natural-language-based prospective cohorts. To address this, we present HealthFound, a medical LLM trained on 12.4 million self-constructed examples. These include 15-year longitudinal biomedical records from 501,936 participants, as well as datasets for medical knowledge and general reasoning. We propose a novel three-stage training framework comprising progressive curriculum supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled retention fine-tuning, and task-verifiable policy optimization. This enables the model to effectively parse heterogeneous quantitative follow-up data and perform robust quantitative reasoning. HealthFound achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple newly constructed benchmarks. It attains the highest accuracy on eight public medical benchmarks for general medical competence. On 1,162 UK Biobank tasks predicting future disease onset from biomedical measurements, it outperforms the second-best model by over 10 percentage points on average. In two independent external validations (MIMIC-IV and NHANES), it demonstrates superior zero-shot generalization, achieving improvements of over 6% across 484 disease endpoints. The model also achieves top results on novel tasks for literature-derived question answering and quantitative indicator imputation. Furthermore, HealthFound generates interpretable reasoning rationales that are consistent with established biomedical knowledge. Collectively, our results demonstrate that HealthFound enables medical LLMs to evolve from static knowledge repositories into dynamic quantitative reasoning engines over longitudinal health data.

papers.title: Which Features of Medication Double-Check Procedures are Considered Desirable and Implemented in Practice? A Cross-Sectional Web-Based Vignette Study among Nurses in Japan
papers.abstract: ObjectiveNurses specific medication-administration double-check procedures vary widely; while independent double-checks (IDCs) are considered effective and recommended, they are implemented insufficiently in practice. This study aimed to classify these procedures by their component features and determine which features nurses consider desirable and perceive as implemented in clinical practice. DesignCross-sectional web-based vignette study Setting, participants, and methodsNurses working in Japanese hospitals or clinics participated in this study, for which we created 84 scenarios by combining checking procedures features, including independence between checkers, across the calculation, preparation, and administration stages. For each scenario, participants self-reported the desirability of the procedure and its perceived implementation frequency in their clinical setting. Linear mixed-effects models assessed associations between checking-procedure features and each rating, and McNemars test assessed discrepancies between desirability and implementation frequency for IDC. Primary outcomeAssociations between double-check procedures features and their desirability and implementation frequency, and the alignment between desirability and implementation frequency for IDC ResultsOf 534 respondents, 265 were analyzed after prespecified attention-check exclusions. Independent checking was positively associated with desirability (b=0.304, 95% CI [0.255, 0.353], p<0.001), perceived implementation frequency for high-risk medications (b=0.140, 95% CI [0.080, 0.200], p<0.001), and non-high-risk medications (b=0.083, 95% CI [0.022, 0.143], p=0.008). Only 22.5% of nurses perceived IDC as the most frequently implemented procedure during the calculation stage. Moreover, 23.4% rated IDC as the most desirable, but did not report it as the most frequently implemented, whereas 8.1% showed the reverse pattern (OR=2.89, 95% CI [1.69, 4.94], p<0.001). ConclusionsAlthough independence, a key feature of IDC, was reflected in nurses desirability ratings and perceived implementation frequency, IDC was not the most frequently implemented checking procedure, relative to others. Implementing IDC may require not only promoting understanding of its significance but also establishing work protocols and organizational environments that enable independent checking.

papers.title: Developing and piloting a discrete choice experiment to assess stakeholder preferences for community-based exercise programmes after stroke
papers.abstract: BackgroundCommunity-based exercise may support physical and cognitive recovery after stroke, but the preferences of stakeholders involved in receiving, supporting and delivering these programmes are poorly understood. This study piloted a discrete choice experiment (DCE) that aimed to evaluate stroke survivors, carers, clinicians, and fitness instructors preferences for community-based exercise programmes for stroke survivors. The pilot aimed to assess the feasibility of conducting and analysing data for a larger-scale study and inform the sample size for a definitive DCE. MethodsA DCE design was developed using literature reviews, stakeholder consultations, and evaluations of current services. Six attributes were included in the design: location, price, session frequency, individualisation, carer involvement, and recovery. Sixteen Bayesian D-optimal choice sets were developed, then blocked into two sets of eight to reduce cognitive burden. Main-effects were analysed using a mixed logit model, and stakeholder differences were explored using a conditional logit interaction model. Willingness to pay was also calculated. ResultsOverall, 161 respondents started the survey and 106 (66%) fully completed it. Stakeholders significantly preferred programmes that were delivered at a leisure centre, lower priced, individualised, had carer-specific sessions and offered greater chances of recovery. The largest willingness-to-pay estimates were {pound}49.41/ month for 80% chance of meaningful recovery vs 20%, and {pound}18.61/ month for leisure centre delivery vs online. Significant preference heterogeneity was identified in the main-effects model. Exploratory stakeholder interactions suggested clinicians were more price sensitive and placed greater importance on recovery and carer-specific sessions than stroke survivors, while fitness instructors placed greater importance on programme location and recovery. Carer interaction estimates were unstable due to the small subgroup sample. ConclusionsThe pilot supported the feasibility of the DCE design and analytical approach but identified limitations in the recruitment methods and survey completion. Addition of face-to-face recruitment methods are recommended for a larger-scale study. A larger sample size is required to investigate differences in preferences between stakeholder groups.

papers.title: From Tumor Board Presence to Documented Review: A Coverage Cascade for Multidisciplinary Cancer Care in India
papers.abstract: BackgroundMultidisciplinary tumor boards (MTBs) are a standard part of cancer care, yet India has no national measure of how many cancer patients are discussed at one. A national survey of hospitals in the National Cancer Registry Programme (NCRP), published in 2026, gives the first structured look at board presence and functioning. ObjectiveTo describe how far hospital-level tumor board presence translates into all-case review, documentation and follow-up, and to define the data needed to measure patient-level coverage. MethodsSecondary analysis of published aggregate data: the ICMR-NCDIR survey of 229 hospitals in the NCRP hospital-based cancer registry (HBCR) network (October 2024), the HBCR 2021 report, national incidence estimates (ICMR-NCDIR 2022; GLOBOCAN 2024) and two published single-center MTB audits. We calculated proportions with Wilson 95% confidence intervals, non-response bounds across all 229 hospitals, and logical bounds for joint conditions. No individual-level data were used. ResultsA total of 229 hospitals were invited and 172 responded (75.1%). Among the respondents, 137 (79.7%; 59.8% to 84.7% across all hospitals) reported a functional tumor board. Only 65 respondents (37.8%; 28.4% to 53.3%) reported boards that review all cases, 71 (41.3%) had a follow-up system, 50 (29.1%) used any electronic documentation and 7 (4.1%) always took part in cross-hospital reviews. The share of hospitals with both all-case review and a follow-up system could lie anywhere from 0% to 37.8% of respondents. Boards were reported more often in private (86.6%) than in public hospitals (72.5%). Two single-center audits reported about 800 case discussions (573 new patients) and 1,260 case discussions (about 917 patients) a year, but neither reported new registrations at the same hospital, so coverage could not be calculated. ConclusionsTumor board presence is common in India, but evidence of all-case review, documentation and follow-up is much thinner, and the share of patients reviewed nationally is unknown. We propose six indicators that hospital-based registries could report to measure coverage directly.

papers.title: The factors associated with stillbirth in urban Vadodara: A population based cross-sectional study, Vadodara Municipal Corporation, Gujarat, India.
papers.abstract: BackgroundStillbirths are a neglected problem in India, and the data we have are often unreliable. This study aimed to assess stillbirth record quality in an urban setting and understand the experiences, health impacts, and perceived causes from both families and health workers. MethodsA mixed-methods study was conducted in Vadodara Municipal Corporation during January- December 2023. All reported stillbirths ([≥]28 weeks or [≥]1000 g) were reviewed. Families were interviewed at home using a standardized questionnaire, with in-depth interviews conducted with 9 families and 17 health workers (doctors, ANMs, ASHAs). Quantitative data were analysed using Excel and Jamovi; qualitative data were analysed thematically. ResultsOf 61 stillbirths reported by VMC, quality audits revealed 7 errors (duplicates/misclassifications) and 2 data entry errors, yielding a true stillbirth rate of 1.7 per 1000 total births. The eastern zone recorded the most cases (21), while the southern zone had the highest rate (4.1 per 1000). Most deliveries occurred in government hospitals (64%). Common reported causes were intrauterine foetal death on routine ultrasound (26%) and premature delivery (19%). Families reported delayed care access, undertrained staff, poor facilities, and challenges accessing government scheme benefits. Health workers identified preventable factors (hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, meconium aspiration, growth restriction, birth defects) and non-preventable factors (extreme prematurity, multiple pregnancy). Interpretation & conclusionsStillbirth data in Vadodara have serious quality problems which can be fixed. Many stillbirths could be avoided with better pregnancy monitoring, better communication, stronger referral systems and more awareness in the community.

papers.title: RMNCH Service Availability and Readiness of Restructured Primary Health-care Facilities in Ethiopia: a multi-region cross-sectional assessment
papers.abstract: BackgroundA responsive and resilient health system that is informed by community needs and guided by evidence-based interventions is fundamental to delivering quality essential health services and achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Ethiopia committed to improve access to and quality of essential health services through the Health Extension Program Optimization (HEPO) roadmap, which restructured primary healthcare facilities into three categories i.e., Basic Health Posts (BHPs), Comprehensive Health Posts (CHPs), and Health Extension Program units imbedded within Health Centers (HCs). However, evidence on the reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health (RMNCH) service availability and readiness of these restructured primary health-care facilities remains limited. MethodsThis multi-region cross-sectional facility based study was conducted between December 2024 and February 2025. A structured questionnaire adapted from the World Health Organization Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) was used to measure service availability, general facility readiness, and RMNCH service-specific readiness using predefined domains and tracer items. Differences across facility types were assessed using Kruskal-Wallis or categorical association tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment for multiple comparisons. Multivariable linear regression estimated the adjusted differences in overall RMNCH readiness, controlling for region, urban-rural residence, and log-transformed catchment population, with robust standard errors clustered at woreda level. ResultsA total of 305 primary health care facilities were assessed, including 107 BHPs (35.1%), 142 CHPs (46.6%), and 56 HCs (18.4%). Nearly all BHPs were located in rural settings (99.1%), compared with 86.6% of CHPs and 71.4% of HCs. The median general health facility readiness were increased significantly across facility levels, from 33.1% (IQR: 24.4-40.7) in BHPs to 62.9% (IQR: 54.1-71.4) in CHPs and 89.6% (IQR: 81.3-93.6) in HCs (p<0.001). And the median overall RMNCH service readiness was 67.9%, 77.8%, and 91.1% for BHPs, CHPs, and HCs, respectively (p<0.001). skilled Birth Attendance readiness was demonstrated the largest gap between facility types. Compared with CHPs, BHPs scored 9.9 percentage points lower in adjusted RMNCH service readiness (95% CI: -14.7 to -5.1; p<0.001), while HCs scored 8.7 points higher (95% CI: 1.7-15.8; p=0.015). ConclusionsThe restructured primary healthcare facilities expanded access to essential services, particularly through CHPs, which occupy an intermediate position between BHPs and HCs through substantial expansion of RMNCH service packages for underserved communities. Nevertheless, significant gaps remain in staffing, infrastructure, commodities, diagnostics, and childbirth readiness. Future HEPO scale-up should prioritize strengthening childbirth-readiness packages and ensuring reliable supply chains for essential medicines and diagnostics.

papers.title: Pretreatment Attrition, Treatment Delay and Treatment Outcome in Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis: A Mixed-Methods Cohort Study in Public and Private Hospitals in Indonesia
papers.abstract: BackgroundDrug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) remains a major problem in Indonesia, with a significant low treatment initiation rate. This study identifies factors influencing treatment initiation and assess the impact of delay on patient outcomes. MethodsWe conducted a mixed-methods study using a parallel convergent design. The quantitative component analyzed the Tuberculosis Information System (TBIS) data from three hospitals in Jakarta and Bogor from January 2022 to December 2023. The qualitative component involved in-depth interviews and Focus Group Discussions (FGD) with DR-TB patients, healthcare workers, patient supporters, and program managers. ResultsAmong 1,665 people with DR-TB included in this study, we found a pre- treatment attrition rate of 6.4%. We identified two factors of pre-treatment attrition: prior TB treatment (aOR=1.7, 95%CI 1.082-2.671) and distance to hospital (aOR=1.9, 95%CI: 1.136-3.180). Conversely, referred patients, treatment in suburban areas, and people with rifampicin-resistant (RR)-TB were 85%, 82%, and 63% less likely to experience attrition, respectively. Qualitative findings identify patient, social, and health system barriers to the treatment initiation, and alternative remedies emerged as a coping mechanism. ConclusionStrengthening referral systems, decentralizing care, and addressing socio- economic barriers are critical for ensuring timely DR-TB treatment initiation.
